The story contains several turns that subvert traditional tropes (making them surprising) while remaining deeply rooted in the characters' pragmatic realities (making them appropriate). 

First, when Nora marries into a wealthy family, both she and the reader expect the classic trope of the snobbish mother-in-law rejecting the working-class bride or offering her a check to disappear. Instead, Miss Emily immediately absorbs and accepts her, treating her like an "underperforming subsidiary" to be restructured. This is surprising, yet entirely appropriate for a pragmatic investment banker who realizes her passive, academic son needs someone grounded in reality.

Second, the ending provides a surprising yet fitting turn in Nora's allegiance. Rather than siding with her gentle husband against his controlling mother, Nora immediately puts Miss Emily’s manipulative plan into action. While this might seem like a sudden betrayal of Julian’s romanticized view of her, it is completely appropriate for Nora's character. Her background as a grocery store cashier has given her a sharp, unsentimental understanding of what things cost and what service entails. She realizes she doesn't want to struggle in Vermont any more than Miss Emily wants her to, making her quiet alliance with her mother-in-law anearned and believable conclusion.
